title: GCP Security Overview
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Understand the shared responsibility model in Google Cloud.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Security in Google Cloud is a shared responsibility. Google secures the underlying physical infrastructure, hardware, and global network, while you are responsible for securing your data, application code, and identity management within the cloud.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud projects get-iam-policy [PROJECT_ID]` # View current project IAM policy

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A company ensuring their customer database is secure by implementing strict IAM roles, even though Google manages the physical security of the data center where the database resides.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Assuming Google handles all security, leading to public buckets or overly permissive firewall rules. You are responsible for the 'Security IN the Cloud'.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Understanding the shared responsibility model is fundamental; always document which security controls are managed by your team versus Google.

[SUMMARY]
- Shared responsibility between Google and the customer.
- Google secures the 'Cloud'; you secure your 'Data'.
- Foundation of all GCP security strategies.
insight: Understanding the shared responsibility model is fundamental to cloud security.

title: IAM Policy Structure
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Understand how IAM policies are structured and inherited.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
An IAM policy is a collection of bindings that link one or more members (users, groups, domains, or service accounts) to a single role. Policies are hierarchical and are inherited from higher levels in the resource hierarchy (Organization -> Folder -> Project -> Resource).

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'IAM policies are represented in JSON or YAML format'` # Data format info

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Granting a 'Developer' group access to a specific 'Project' folder, which automatically gives them access to all projects inside that folder due to inheritance.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Not realizing that a 'Viewer' role at the Organization level cannot be revoked at the Project level. Inheritance is additive and cannot be 'blocked' lower down.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Policies are hierarchical; always apply permissions at the lowest possible level to minimize the blast radius of any single account.

[SUMMARY]
- Policy = Members + Role.
- Hierarchical inheritance (Org down to Resource).
- Represented as JSON or YAML objects.
insight: Policies are hierarchical and are inherited from higher levels (Org -> Folder -> Project).

lab.command: echo 'IAM policies are represented in JSON or YAML format'
lab.output: IAM policies are represented in JSON or YAML format

title: IAM Conditions
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Implement context-aware security using IAM conditions.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
IAM Conditions allow you to grant access only if specific criteria are met. This adds an extra layer of context-aware security, allowing permissions to be restricted based on request timing (e.g., 'only during business hours') or resource attributes (e.g., 'only resources with a specific tag').

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Configure conditions in the Console or via gcloud with --condition'` # Management info

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Granting temporary 'Storage Admin' access to a contractor, but only for the duration of their 3-month contract using a date/time condition.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Creating overly complex conditions that are difficult to audit. Keep conditions simple and well-documented to avoid accidental lockouts.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Conditions add an extra layer of context-aware security; use them for 'Just-in-Time' access or to enforce time-based security policies.

[SUMMARY]
- Attribute-based access control.
- Restricts roles based on time, resource, or context.
- Enhances the 'Least Privilege' model.
insight: Conditions add an extra layer of context-aware security to your IAM policies.

lab.command: echo 'Configure conditions in the Console or via gcloud with --condition'
lab.output: Configure conditions in the Console or via gcloud with --condition

title: Predefined Roles
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Use Google-maintained roles for granular access control.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Predefined roles are created and maintained by Google. They provide granular access to specific services (e.g., `roles/storage.objectViewer`) and are automatically updated as new features and permissions are added to the service.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud iam roles list --filter='name:roles/storage.'` # Search for storage roles

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Assigning the `roles/compute.instanceAdmin` role to a DevOps engineer so they can manage VMs without giving them full 'Editor' access to the entire project.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Using 'Basic Roles' (Owner, Editor, Viewer) in production. These are too broad and violate the principle of least privilege.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always prefer predefined roles over basic roles for better granularity and to minimize the risk of accidental resource changes.

[SUMMARY]
- Granular, service-specific roles.
- Maintained and updated by Google.
- Recommended for standard production access.
insight: Always prefer predefined roles over basic roles (Owner, Editor, Viewer) for better granularity.

title: Custom Roles
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Create specialized roles for unique permission requirements.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Custom roles allow you to define a precise set of permissions when predefined roles are either too broad or too restrictive. They are maintained by you and only exist within the specific project or organization where they were created.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud iam roles create [ID] --project=[PROJECT] --file=role.yaml` # Create custom role

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Creating a 'Log-Only' role for a security auditor that only includes the specific permissions to view logs and nothing else in the project.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Creating too many custom roles, which increases management overhead. Google adds new permissions to predefined roles, but NOT to your custom ones.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Custom roles are maintained by you; regularly audit them to ensure they still meet security requirements and include necessary new permissions.

[SUMMARY]
- Fully customizable permission sets.
- Project or Organization scoped.
- Requires manual maintenance as services evolve.
insight: Custom roles are maintained by you and only exist within the project or organization where they were created.

title: Service Accounts
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Manage identities for applications and workloads.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
A service account is a special type of Google account that belongs to an application or a VM rather than an individual. It is both an 'identity' (used to authenticate to APIs) and a 'resource' (which can have its own IAM policy controlling who can use it).

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud iam service-accounts list` # List all service accounts
* `gcloud iam service-accounts create [NAME]` # Create new SA

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A Compute Engine VM running a web-app that uses a Service Account to write logs to Cloud Logging without needing a human user's credentials.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Using the default 'Compute Engine default service account', which has the broad 'Editor' role by default. Always create custom SAs with minimal permissions.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Service accounts are the backbone of non-human identity in GCP; treat them as sensitive resources and apply the principle of least privilege.

[SUMMARY]
- Identity for non-human workloads.
- Act as both an identity and a resource.
- Recommended for all automated tasks and app-to-app auth.
insight: Service accounts are both an 'identity' and a 'resource' that can have its own IAM policy.

title: Service Account Keys
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Understand the risks and management of static SA keys.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Service account keys are long-lived cryptographic credentials used for authentication outside of Google Cloud. Because they are static and stored on disk, they represent a significant security risk if stolen or accidentally leaked.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud iam service-accounts keys create [FILE].json --iam-account=[EMAIL]` # Create key

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Using a service account key on a legacy on-premises server to allow it to upload nightly backups to a Cloud Storage bucket.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Committing service account keys to GitHub or public repositories. This is the #1 cause of cloud account compromises.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Avoid downloading keys whenever possible; use Workload Identity (GKE) or attach the SA directly to a VM to avoid handling static credentials.

[SUMMARY]
- Static credentials for external auth.
- High security risk if leaked.
- Should be avoided in favor of managed identities (Workload Identity).
insight: Avoid downloading keys; use Workload Identity or attach the SA directly to a VM instead.

lab.command: gcloud iam service-accounts keys create key.json --iam-account=my-app-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com

title: Service Account Impersonation
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Grant temporary access to SA identities without keys.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Impersonation allows a user or another service account to 'act as' a service account. This is more secure than using static keys because it generates short-lived, temporary access tokens. It requires the 'Service Account Token Creator' role on the target SA.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud config set auth/impersonate_service_account [SA_EMAIL]` # Impersonate via CLI

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A developer needs to test a script locally that requires 'BigQuery Admin' access. Instead of having that role directly, they impersonate a dedicated 'BigQuery-SA'.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Forgetting to revoke the 'impersonate' setting in gcloud config, leading to confusing permission errors in subsequent tasks.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use impersonation for administrative tasks and testing to eliminate the need for sensitive, long-lived JSON key files.

[SUMMARY]
- Short-lived token generation.
- No static keys required.
- Requires 'Service Account Token Creator' role.
insight: Requires the 'Service Account Token Creator' role on the target service account.

title: Workload Identity (GKE)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Securely link GKE pods to GCP identities.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Workload Identity is the recommended way for GKE workloads to access GCP services. It links a Kubernetes Service Account to a Google Cloud Service Account. This allows pods to authenticate to GCP APIs without any secrets or keys stored inside the container.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Configure via GKE cluster and IAM policy bindings'` # Configuration info

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A containerized microservice in GKE that needs to read from Pub/Sub. By using Workload Identity, the pod automatically gets a token with the necessary permissions.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Using node-level service accounts, which gives EVERY pod on that node the same permissions. Workload Identity provides granular, per-pod security.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Ensures that your containers only have the specific permissions they need, without managing secrets or rotating keys manually.

[SUMMARY]
- Gold standard for GKE security.
- Maps K8s SA to GCP SA.
- Eliminates the need for secret management for API access.
insight: Ensures that your containers only have the specific permissions they need, without managing secrets.

lab.command: echo 'Configure via GKE cluster and IAM policy bindings'
lab.output: Configure via GKE cluster and IAM policy bindings

title: Cloud KMS Overview
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Manage cryptographic keys in a hosted service.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Cloud Key Management Service (KMS) allows you to create, use, rotate, and destroy cryptographic keys. It supports both symmetric and asymmetric encryption and is used to manage Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) for other GCP services.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud kms keyrings list --location=[LOCATION]` # List key rings

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Encrypting sensitive PII (Personally Identifiable Information) in a Cloud Storage bucket using a key that you manage and control in KMS.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Thinking KMS is for storing passwords. KMS is for managing cryptographic KEYS; use Secret Manager for storing secrets like passwords and API keys.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use KMS for encrypting sensitive data at rest using your own keys (CMEK) to meet strict regulatory and compliance requirements.

[SUMMARY]
- Managed cryptographic key management.
- Supports rotation and versioning.
- Used for CMEK (Customer-Managed Encryption Keys).
insight: Use KMS for encrypting sensitive data at rest using your own keys (CMEK).

title: Key Rings and Keys
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Understand the hierarchy of KMS resources.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
A Key Ring is a logical grouping of Keys in a specific location. Keys are the actual resources used to perform cryptographic operations like encryption and decryption. Key rings cannot be deleted, but individual keys can be 'destroyed' (scheduled for deletion).

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud kms keys create [KEY] --location=[LOC] --keyring=[RING] --purpose=encryption` # Create key

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Organizing your keys into rings based on environment (e.g., 'prod-ring' and 'dev-ring') or application to simplify IAM access control for different keys.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Creating too many key rings. Since they cannot be deleted, your project can become cluttered with unused ring names over time.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Key Rings cannot be deleted, but individual Keys can be destroyed. Always plan your key naming and ring structure carefully before implementation.

[SUMMARY]
- Key Ring = Collection of Keys.
- Keys = Perform encryption/decryption.
- Immutable container structure (Rings).
insight: Key Rings cannot be deleted, but individual Keys can be destroyed.

title: Envelope Encryption
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Understand the standard model for cloud data encryption.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Envelope encryption uses a Data Encryption Key (DEK) to encrypt the actual data, and then uses a Key Encryption Key (KEK) from KMS to encrypt the DEK. This allows for high-performance local encryption while keeping the master key safe in the cloud.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'KMS manages the KEK; the DEK encrypts the data'` # Process info

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A large database encrypting every row with a unique DEK, but protecting all those DEKs with a single KEK stored in Cloud KMS for centralized control.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Trying to send massive amounts of data directly to KMS for encryption. KMS has size limits; use envelope encryption for large files or high-volume data.

[BEST PRACTICE]
KMS is used to manage the KEK (Key Encryption Key), while your application manages the DEK (Data Encryption Key) locally for performance.

[SUMMARY]
- DEK encrypts data.
- KEK (in KMS) encrypts the DEK.
- Scalable and secure pattern for large datasets.
insight: KMS is used to manage the KEK, while your application manages the DEK.

lab.command: echo 'KMS manages the KEK; the DEK encrypts the data'
lab.output: KMS manages the KEK; the DEK encrypts the data

title: Secret Manager Overview
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Securely store and manage sensitive configuration data.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Secret Manager is a secure storage system for sensitive information like API keys, passwords, and certificates. It provides versioning, audit logging, and fine-grained access control, making it much safer than environment variables or config files.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud secrets list` # List all secrets in project

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Storing a database password in Secret Manager so it can be dynamically retrieved by an application at runtime, ensuring the password never appears in plain text in the code.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Using KMS for passwords or API keys. KMS is for encryption; Secret Manager is the correct tool for managing and retrieving the actual secret values.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Provides versioning, audit logging, and fine-grained access control for secrets. Use it as a central source of truth for all sensitive app config.

[SUMMARY]
- Managed secret storage (passwords, keys).
- Supports versioning and rotation.
- Integrated with IAM for access control.
insight: Provides versioning, audit logging, and fine-grained access control for secrets.

lab.output:
NAME      CREATED              REPLICATION_POLICY  LOCATIONS

title: Creating a Secret
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Provision and configure secrets in Secret Manager.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
You create a secret to hold sensitive data. Each secret can have multiple versions, allowing you to rotate credentials safely. You can also specify replication policies to ensure secrets are available globally or only in specific regions.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud secrets create [NAME] --replication-policy=automatic` # Create secret
* `gcloud secrets versions add [NAME] --data-file=[FILE]` # Add version data

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Creating a 'Stripe-API-Key' secret and adding a new version every time you rotate the key in your Stripe dashboard to ensure zero downtime for your app.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Deleting a secret when you only meant to delete a version. Deleting the secret removes all history and all versions permanently.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Secret Manager handles replication and availability of your secrets globally by default. Use 'automatic' replication unless data residency is required.

[SUMMARY]
- Secrets can have multiple versions.
- Global or Regional replication available.
- `gcloud secrets create` is the starting point.
insight: Secret Manager handles replication and availability of your secrets globally or in specific regions.

title: Accessing a Secret
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Retrieve secret values securely from applications.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
To retrieve a secret, an identity needs the `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` role. You can access specific versions by number or use the `latest` alias to always get the most current value.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret=[NAME]` # Get latest secret value

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A Python application using the Google Cloud Client Library to fetch the `latest` version of the 'db-password' secret during its startup phase.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Granting the 'Accessor' role at the project level. Always grant it on the SPECIFIC secret resource to follow the principle of least privilege.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always reference secrets by version number in production for stability, or use the 'latest' alias in development for easier rotation testing.

[SUMMARY]
- Requires 'Secret Accessor' role.
- Versioned access (number or 'latest').
- Values retrieved via API, never stored on disk.
insight: Always reference secrets by version number or the 'latest' alias in your code.

title: Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Control access to applications without a VPN.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
IAP acts as a central authentication and authorization layer for your web applications and VMs. It verifies user identity via Google accounts and checks IAM policies before allowing traffic through, eliminating the need for a traditional VPN.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Configure in Security -> Identity-Aware Proxy'` # Management info

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Providing secure access to an internal HR portal for employees working from home, without requiring them to sign into a VPN or exposing the portal to the public internet.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Forgetting that IAP only protects the 'entry' point. You still need to ensure your backend services are correctly configured to trust IAP headers.

[BEST PRACTICE]
IAP works by verifying the user's identity via Google accounts and then checking IAM policies. It is a core component of a zero-trust architecture.

[SUMMARY]
- VPN-less access to internal resources.
- Uses Google identities and IAM.
- Protects HTTP applications and SSH/RDP access.
insight: IAP works by verifying the user's identity via Google accounts and then checking IAM policies.

title: IAP for TCP Forwarding
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Provide secure administrative access to private VMs.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
IAP can tunnel TCP traffic, providing secure SSH and RDP access to VMs that do not have external IP addresses. This 'IAP Tunneling' is more secure than using public IPs or maintaining complex bastion hosts.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute ssh [VM] --zone=[ZONE] --tunnel-through-iap` # SSH to private VM

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
An administrator SSHing into a private database VM to perform maintenance, without the VM ever being exposed to the public internet.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Not allowing the GCP IAP IP range (35.235.240.0/20) in your ingress firewall rules. The tunnel will fail if this range is blocked on port 22 or 3389.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Eliminates the need for public IPs or bastion hosts for administrative access. Use IAP for TCP for all VM management tasks.

[SUMMARY]
- Secure SSH/RDP to private VMs.
- Replaces bastion hosts/jump boxes.
- Requires specific firewall rule for IAP IP range.
insight: Eliminates the need for public IPs or bastion hosts for administrative access.

lab.output: Connecting to my-vm via IAP tunnel...

title: VPC Service Controls
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Define security perimeters for sensitive data.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
VPC Service Controls allow you to define a security perimeter around your GCP resources (like Storage or BigQuery). This ensures that data cannot be moved outside the perimeter to untrusted locations, mitigating the risk of data exfiltration by malicious insiders or compromised accounts.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Create perimeters via Security -> VPC Service Controls'` # Management info

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A financial company creating a perimeter around their production BigQuery dataset to ensure that no one can copy that data to a personal GCP project or an external bucket.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Thinking IAM is enough. IAM controls WHO can access data; VPC Service Controls control WHERE that data can go.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Ensures that data cannot be moved out of the perimeter to untrusted locations or projects. Use this for your most sensitive data workloads.

[SUMMARY]
- Data exfiltration protection.
- Logical perimeter around cloud services.
- Goes beyond IAM by restricting data movement.
insight: Ensures that data cannot be moved out of the perimeter to untrusted locations or projects.

lab.command: echo 'Create perimeters via Security -> VPC Service Controls'
lab.output: Create perimeters via Security -> VPC Service Controls

title: Cloud Armor Security Policies
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Protect web applications from DDoS and common attacks.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Cloud Armor works with HTTP(S) Load Balancers to filter traffic based on IP, geography, or custom expressions (WAF rules). It can block common attacks like SQL injection and Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) before they reach your backend.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute security-policies create [NAME] --description=[DESC]` # Create policy

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Blocking all traffic from a specific country where you have no customers but are seeing high volumes of suspicious login attempts.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Not testing new rules before applying them. Use the 'Preview' mode to see what traffic WOULD be blocked without actually stopping it.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use Cloud Armor to protect your applications from DDoS attacks and common web vulnerabilities. It is an essential part of Layer 7 security.

[SUMMARY]
- WAF and DDoS protection for LBs.
- IP, Geo, and Pattern-based filtering.
- Integrated with Google's global infrastructure for massive scale.
insight: Use Cloud Armor to protect your applications from DDoS attacks and common web vulnerabilities.

lab.command: gcloud compute security-policies create block-ips --description='Block malicious IPs'

title: Security Command Center (SCC)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Centralize security and risk management for your organization.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
SCC is a comprehensive security management platform. it automatically discovers resources, detects vulnerabilities (like open firewall ports), and identifies threats (like malware or anomalous activity) across your entire GCP organization.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'View findings in Security -> Security Command Center'` # Management info

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A CISO using the SCC dashboard to see all 'High' severity security findings, such as public Cloud Storage buckets, across the entire company in one view.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Ignoring SCC findings. SCC provides actionable intelligence; failing to remediate 'Critical' findings leaves your environment exposed to known risks.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Provides a centralized dashboard for viewing security findings and compliance status. Review SCC findings daily for production environments.

[SUMMARY]
- Centralized security hub.
- Automated vulnerability and threat detection.
- Monitors compliance with standard security frameworks.
insight: Provides a centralized dashboard for viewing security findings and compliance status.

lab.command: echo 'View findings in Security -> Security Command Center'
lab.output: View findings in Security -> Security Command Center

title: Cloud Data Loss Prevention (DLP)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Discover and protect sensitive data in your datasets.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Cloud DLP allows you to identify and classify sensitive data like PII (names, emails), credit card numbers, and social security numbers. It can then de-identify or mask that data to prevent accidental exposure.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Create inspection jobs via Security -> Data Loss Prevention'` # Management info

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Scanning a BigQuery table before sharing it with a data science team to ensure that all customer names and emails are masked or replaced with tokens.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Thinking DLP only works on text. DLP can also scan images for sensitive data (e.g., a photo of a credit card or a driver's license).

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use DLP to de-identify or mask sensitive data before sharing it with other teams or services to minimize the risk of data leakage.

[SUMMARY]
- PII discovery and classification.
- Data masking and de-identification.
- Essential for privacy and compliance (GDPR, HIPAA).
insight: Use DLP to de-identify or mask sensitive data before sharing it with other teams or services.

lab.command: echo 'Create inspection jobs via Security -> Data Loss Prevention'
lab.output: Create inspection jobs via Security -> Data Loss Prevention

title: IAM Recommender
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Automate the application of the principle of least privilege.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
The IAM Recommender analyzes your project's role usage and identifies users with permissions they aren't using. It then provides automated recommendations to replace broad roles (like 'Editor') with more specific, granular roles.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud recommender recommendations list --recommender=google.iam.policy.Recommender --project=[PROJ] --location=global` # List IAM tips

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A project owner receiving a recommendation to change a user's role from 'Project Editor' to 'Storage Object Viewer' because they only accessed storage buckets in the last 90 days.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Blindly applying recommendations without checking if the user might need those permissions for rare, periodic tasks (like monthly audits).

[BEST PRACTICE]
Review and apply recommendations regularly to reduce your project's attack surface and enforce the principle of least privilege automatically.

[SUMMARY]
- Identifies over-privileged users.
- Suggests granular role replacements.
- Helps maintain a secure 'Least Privilege' posture.
insight: Review and apply recommendations regularly to reduce your project's attack surface.

title: Organization Policies
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Enforce global security constraints across all resources.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Organization Policies give you centralized, programmatic control over your resources. You can enforce guardrails across your entire organization, such as 'disallowing external IPs on VMs' or 'restricting the regions where resources can be created'.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud resource-manager org-policies list --organization=[ORG_ID]` # List active policies

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A global security policy that prevents any developer in any project from creating a VM with a public IP address, forcing all access through IAP.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Setting a policy at the root that breaks legitimate use cases in specific projects. Use 'Policy Exclusions' sparingly at lower folder levels if needed.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Enforce policies like 'disable external IP addresses' or 'restrict allowed regions' globally to maintain a consistent security posture.

[SUMMARY]
- Global guardrails for GCP resources.
- Overrides project-level settings.
- Essential for compliance and organization-wide governance.
insight: Enforce policies like 'disable external IP addresses' or 'restrict allowed regions' globally.
next: Service Control Policies (SCPs) vs Org Policies

title: Resource Manager Organization
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Understand the root of the GCP resource hierarchy.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
The Organization resource is the root node of the Google Cloud resource hierarchy. It allows for centralized management of all resources, users, and billing. It is required for advanced features like Folders and Organization Policies.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud organizations list` # List all organizations you have access to

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A company using the Organization resource to centrally manage 500 different projects, ensuring that billing and security policies are applied consistently to all of them.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Operating without an Organization resource (using just isolated projects). This makes centralized auditing and security management almost impossible as the company grows.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Requires a Google Workspace or Cloud Identity account to create an Organization. Set this up as the first step of any professional GCP deployment.

[SUMMARY]
- Root node of the hierarchy.
- Enables centralized governance.
- Tied to Cloud Identity or Google Workspace.
insight: Requires a Google Workspace or Cloud Identity account to create an Organization.

title: IAM Best Practices: Groups
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Simplify identity management using Google Groups.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Always manage access using Google Groups instead of granting roles to individual users. When a team member joins or leaves, you only need to update the group membership, and their access is automatically updated across all linked projects.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Add users to groups in the Google Admin Console'` # Management info

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
An employee moving from the 'Dev' team to the 'Security' team. By moving them from the 'dev-group' to the 'security-group', their permissions are updated instantly everywhere.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Granting roles directly to user emails. This creates 'ghost permissions' when users leave the company and makes it extremely difficult to audit who has access to what.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Updating group membership automatically updates access for all group members across all projects. It is much cleaner and more scalable than individual assignments.

[SUMMARY]
- Group-based access control.
- Easier to audit and maintain.
- Recommended for all production environments.
insight: Updating group membership automatically updates access for all group members across all projects.

title: IAM Best Practices: Least Privilege
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Minimize the risk of security breaches using minimal permissions.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
The principle of least privilege means granting only the minimum permissions required for a user or service account to perform its specific task. This limits the potential damage if an account is compromised.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Use predefined or custom roles instead of basic roles'` # Role selection tip

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Giving a CI/CD service account only the 'Cloud Run Developer' role instead of 'Project Editor', so it can deploy code but cannot delete the VPC or modify IAM policies.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Using 'Owner' or 'Editor' roles for day-to-day work. These roles are extremely powerful and should be reserved only for a few highly trusted administrators.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Least privilege reduces the impact of compromised credentials. Regularly audit roles and remove any that are no longer strictly necessary.

[SUMMARY]
- Grant minimum needed permissions.
- Avoid 'Basic Roles' (Owner/Editor).
- Essential for reducing 'Blast Radius'.
insight: Least privilege reduces the impact of compromised credentials.

title: Cloud Identity Overview
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Manage users and groups in a centralized IDaaS.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Cloud Identity is an Identity as a Service (IDaaS) that serves as the core authentication provider for GCP. it allows you to manage users and groups independently of Google Workspace, providing SSO and MFA capabilities.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Manage identities in Google Admin Console'` # Management info

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A company using Cloud Identity to sync their users from Microsoft Active Directory, allowing employees to use their corporate passwords to sign into the GCP console.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Managing 'Gmail' accounts for corporate cloud access. Professional deployments should always use Cloud Identity or Google Workspace for better control.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Supports Single Sign-On (SSO) with third-party providers like Azure AD and Okta, which simplifies the user experience and centralizes security.

[SUMMARY]
- Managed identity provider for GCP.
- Supports SSO and MFA.
- Foundation for the Organization resource.
insight: Supports Single Sign-On (SSO) with third-party providers like Azure AD and Okta.

title: Access Context Manager
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Implement zero-trust access control based on context.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Access Context Manager allows you to define fine-grained access levels based on the user's request context, such as their IP range, device security state (e.g., 'must be encrypted'), or geographic location.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud access-context-manager levels list --policy=[POLICY_ID]` # List access levels

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Restricting access to the billing project so it can only be accessed from the corporate office IP range and only from company-managed laptops.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Creating 'impossible' levels that lock everyone out. Always test your access levels with a small group of users before applying them broadly.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Define 'access levels' based on IP range, device state, or user identity to move beyond simple password-based security.

[SUMMARY]
- Context-aware access control.
- Foundation for BeyondCorp (Zero Trust).
- Uses attributes like IP, Device, and Location.
insight: Define 'access levels' based on IP range, device state, or user identity.

title: OS Login
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Manage SSH access to VMs using IAM roles.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
OS Login allows you to use IAM roles to manage SSH access to your Compute Engine instances. It links a user's Linux profile to their Google identity, eliminating the need to manually manage and distribute individual SSH keys.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute project-info add-metadata --metadata enable-oslogin=TRUE` # Enable OS Login

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A company where the 'Security' team grants or revokes SSH access to production VMs simply by adding or removing an IAM role for a user.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Continuing to use metadata-based SSH keys after enabling OS Login. Metadata keys can be less secure and harder to audit than OS Login identities.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Provides centralized lifecycle management of SSH access for your team, ensuring that when a user loses their IAM role, they instantly lose VM access.

[SUMMARY]
- IAM-based SSH management.
- No more manual SSH key distribution.
- Centralized and auditable VM access.
insight: Provides centralized lifecycle management of SSH access for your team.

title: Binary Authorization Overview
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Ensure only trusted container images are deployed.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Binary Authorization ensures that only trusted container images are deployed to GKE or Cloud Run. It requires 'signatures' (attestations) from authorized attestors, ensuring the image hasn't been tampered with and has passed security scans.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Configure policies in Security -> Binary Authorization'` # Management info

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A production environment that only allows containers that have been 'signed' by the automated security scanning tool in the CI/CD pipeline.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Not having an 'Emergency Bypass' (Breakglass) procedure. If your signing system fails, you might be unable to deploy critical security fixes without a bypass.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Prevents the deployment of unverified or malicious images in your production environment. Use it as part of a secure CI/CD pipeline.

[SUMMARY]
- Deploy-time verification for containers.
- Requires signatures from trusted attestors.
- Critical for 'Secure Supply Chain' compliance.
insight: Prevents the deployment of unverified or malicious images in your production environment.

title: Secret Rotation
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Automate the replacement of sensitive credentials.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Secret Manager supports automatic rotation of secrets. It triggers a Cloud Function on a schedule to update the credential in both the Secret Manager and the target service (e.g., changing a database password).

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Configure rotation period and Cloud Function in Secret settings'` # Management info

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Automatically rotating the password for a Cloud SQL database every 30 days, ensuring that if a password is ever leaked, it is only valid for a limited time.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Rotating secrets without testing the application's ability to pick up the new value. Ensure your app logic can handle 'hot' credential updates.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Regularly rotating secrets reduces the window of opportunity for stolen credentials to be used by an attacker.

[SUMMARY]
- Automated credential replacement.
- Triggered via Cloud Functions.
- Minimizes the impact of credential leakage.
insight: Regularly rotating secrets reduces the window of opportunity for stolen credentials.

title: Firewall Rules Logging
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Audit network traffic allowed or denied by firewall rules.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Firewall rules logging records every connection that was allowed or denied by a specific rule. This provides a detailed audit trail of all network traffic attempting to enter or leave your VPC.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute firewall-rules update [RULE_NAME] --enable-logging` # Enable logging on rule

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Investigating a suspected brute-force attack by reviewing firewall logs to see thousands of 'Denied' connection attempts on port 22 from a single IP address.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Enabling logging on all rules in a high-traffic environment, which can generate a massive amount of log data and increase your logging bill significantly.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use firewall logs to audit network traffic and identify potential security threats or misconfigurations in your network security rules.

[SUMMARY]
- Logs every connection (allow or deny).
- Essential for network forensics.
- Should be used selectively on critical rules to manage costs.
insight: Use firewall logs to audit network traffic and identify potential security threats or misconfigurations.

title: Cloud KMS Key Rotation
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Automate the lifecycle of encryption keys.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
You can configure Cloud KMS to automatically rotate encryption keys on a schedule (e.g., every 90 days). Each rotation creates a new 'Key Version', and KMS handles the complexity of managing multiple versions for you.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud kms keys update [KEY] --location=[LOC] --keyring=[RING] --rotation-period=90d --next-rotation-time=[DATE]` # Set rotation

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Meeting a compliance requirement that all master encryption keys must be rotated at least once every quarter, without manually recreating keys each time.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Not understanding that old key versions are kept. If you encrypt data with Version 1 and then rotate to Version 2, KMS still needs Version 1 to decrypt that old data.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Automating key rotation helps comply with security standards and reduces the risk associated with a compromised key version.

[SUMMARY]
- Scheduled replacement of encryption keys.
- Creates new key versions automatically.
- Essential for compliance and risk reduction.
insight: Automating key rotation helps comply with security standards and best practices.

title: Access Approval
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Control Google personnel access to your data.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Access Approval ensures that Google personnel must have your explicit approval before they can access your data or configurations for troubleshooting purposes. It adds a layer of human control over Google's administrative access.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Enable in Security -> Access Approval'` # Management info

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A highly regulated bank requiring that any time a Google support engineer needs to look at their project configuration, a bank security officer must first 'Approve' the request.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Thinking Google engineers can access your data at any time. By default, access is highly restricted; Access Approval makes that restriction visible and controllable by you.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Adds an extra layer of control over your data, ensuring that access only happens when you explicitly request and approve it.

[SUMMARY]
- Human-in-the-loop control for Google access.
- Essential for high-compliance environments.
- Provides an audit trail of all approved access requests.
insight: Adds an extra layer of control over your data, ensuring that access only happens when you request it.

title: Security Health Analytics
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Automatically detect cloud misconfigurations.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Security Health Analytics (part of SCC) automatically scans your environment for common security misconfigurations, such as public buckets, open firewall ports, and missing audit logs. It provides 'findings' with clear remediation steps.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'View findings in SCC dashboard'` # Management info

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Automatically discovering that a new developer accidentally left an RDP port open to the entire internet on a Windows VM, allowing for immediate remediation.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Ignoring the 'Low' severity findings. While 'Critical' findings are the priority, 'Low' findings often represent the first steps in a more complex attack path.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Detects issues like public buckets and open ports automatically; treat SCC findings as a high-priority 'To-Do' list for your security team.

[SUMMARY]
- Automated misconfiguration scanning.
- Provides findings and remediation tips.
- Essential for maintaining a secure environment at scale.
insight: Detects issues like public buckets, open firewall ports, and missing audit logs.

title: BeyondCorp Enterprise
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Implement zero-trust security for all users and apps.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
BeyondCorp is Google's zero-trust implementation. it moves security from the network perimeter to individual users and devices. Every request is authenticated and authorized based on real-time device health and user context.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Integrated with IAP and Access Context Manager'` # Component info

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Allowing employees to securely access company apps from anywhere in the world without a VPN, as long as their laptop is company-managed and they have MFA active.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Thinking zero-trust means 'no security'. It actually means 'continuous security' where trust is never assumed and always verified.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Moves security from the network perimeter to individual users and devices, providing better protection against modern, mobile-first threats.

[SUMMARY]
- Zero-trust security model.
- No VPN required for secure access.
- Trust is based on identity and context, not network location.
insight: Moves security from the network perimeter to individual users and devices.

title: Cloud IDS
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Detect network-level threats in your VPC.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Cloud Intrusion Detection System (IDS) provides managed network security that detects malware, spyware, and command-and-control attacks. It uses Palo Alto Networks technology to inspect a mirror copy of your VPC traffic without affecting performance.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud ids endpoints list --region=[REGION]` # List IDS endpoints

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Detecting a compromised VM that is attempting to communicate with a known malicious command-and-control server on the internet.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Thinking IDS 'blocks' traffic. Cloud IDS is for DETECTION; use Cloud Armor or Firewall rules to actually BLOCK malicious traffic.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Uses Palo Alto Networks technology to inspect mirrored traffic, providing deep visibility into network-level threats without impacting application latency.

[SUMMARY]
- Managed network threat detection.
- Inspects mirrored VPC traffic.
- Identifies malware and command-and-control activity.
insight: Uses Palo Alto Networks technology to inspect mirrored traffic in your VPC.

title: Troubleshooting IAM Policies
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Analyze and resolve complex permission issues.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
The IAM Policy Troubleshooter helps you understand why a user has (or doesn't have) a specific permission on a resource. It accounts for role inheritance, conditions, and service-specific access controls.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Access via IAM -> Policy Troubleshooter in the Console'` # Management info

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Diagnosing why a developer can't upload to a bucket despite having the 'Storage Object Creator' role (e.g., finding that a Deny policy or a condition is blocking them).

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Only checking project-level roles. Permissions can be granted (or denied) at many levels; always use the troubleshooter for a definitive answer.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Accounts for role inheritance, conditions, and service-specific permissions, making it the most accurate tool for resolving access issues.

[SUMMARY]
- Root-cause analysis for IAM issues.
- Evaluates inheritance and conditions.
- Saves hours of manual permission checking.
insight: Accounts for role inheritance, conditions, and service-specific permissions.

title: Shielded VM Security
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Ensure the integrity of your VM boot process.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Shielded VMs provide verifiable integrity for your instances using features like Secure Boot, Virtual Trusted Platform Module (vTPM), and integrity monitoring. This protects against rootkits and boot-level malware.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute instances describe [VM] --zone=[ZONE] --format='value(shieldedInstanceConfig)'` # Check VM security

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A government agency requiring that all cloud VMs have 'Secure Boot' enabled to prevent unauthorized kernels or drivers from loading during the boot process.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Disabling vTPM or Secure Boot to run unverified custom drivers. This compromises the integrity of the VM and is not recommended for production.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Protects against boot-level and kernel-level rootkits and malware. Always use Shielded VM images for production workloads.

[SUMMARY]
- Boot-level integrity verification.
- Secure Boot and vTPM features.
- Essential for high-security and regulated workloads.
insight: Protects against boot-level and kernel-level rootkits and malware.

title: Conclusion: Security on GCP
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Finalize your knowledge of Google Cloud security tools and practices.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Security is an ongoing process of monitoring, hardening, and adapting to new threats. You've mastered IAM, encryption, secret management, and threat detection. These tools provide a multi-layered defense-in-depth for your cloud environment.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud projects get-iam-policy [PROJECT_ID] --limit=1` # Final security audit check

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A lead security engineer reviewing the entire project's security posture, ensuring that all 'Least Privilege' and 'Defense-in-Depth' principles are active.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Thinking security is 'done'. As new threats emerge and applications change, your security configuration must be continuously reviewed and updated.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Security is an ongoing process; regularly audit your IAM, network, and storage configurations using automated tools like SCC and IAM Recommender.

[SUMMARY]
- Comprehensive mastery of GCP security suite.
- Multi-layered defense (IAM, Network, Data).
- Foundation for a secure and compliant cloud architecture.
insight: Security is an ongoing process of monitoring, hardening, and adapting to new threats.
